1.title: Reflected Images
1.text:
Reflected Images

A clear reflected image needs a smooth reflecting surface.

Our big question for this lesson: why does light bouncing off a mirror make an image, while light bouncing off a sheet of paper does not? Let's start at the edge of a pond.

When the water is perfectly still, you can see a crisp reflection. But wind ripples or a passing boat's waves disturb the surface, and the reflection turns blurry and broken up, like in Figure 1. The light still reflects, but not in a way that forms a clear image.

People have known this for a long time. Almost 4000 years ago, Egyptians used polished metal mirrors to see themselves. Artisans in sixteenth-century Venice coated the back of flat glass with a thin sheet of metal. But truly sharp mirrors arrived in 1857, when the French scientist Jean Foucault found a way to coat glass with silver. Today, mirrors are made by evaporating aluminum or silver onto highly polished glass, and they sit inside lasers, telescopes, and other precise optical tools. The same physics governs them all.

2.title: Your Investigation Toolkit
2.text:
Your Investigation Toolkit

Collect evidence in your Science Journal and investigate with activities.

Use your Science Journal to record the evidence you collect as you work through the readings and activities in this lesson.

Online, the Forensics Lab called A Little Time to Reflect has you investigate how the angle at which light hits a plane mirror relates to the angle at which it bounces off. As you read, build a table of crosscutting concepts and fill in examples you find along the way.

3.title: The Law of Reflection
3.text:
The Law of Reflection

The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal: theta sub r equals theta sub i.

Figure 2 shows a light ray striking a reflecting surface. To describe it, we use the normal, an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface right where the light hits. The incoming ray is the incident ray, and the outgoing ray is the reflected ray.

Here's the neat part. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal all lie in the same plane, which is perpendicular to the surface. So even though light travels in three dimensions, reflection itself is flat, or planar.

The law of reflection says the angle the reflected ray makes with the normal equals the angle the incident ray makes with that same normal. In symbols, theta sub r equals theta sub i, where theta sub r is the angle of reflection and theta sub i is the angle of incidence.

4.title: Reflection in the Wave Model
4.text:
Reflection in the Wave Model

Every point on a wavefront travels the same distance in the same time, so the wavefront leaves at the same angle it arrived.

We can also explain the law of reflection with the wave model of light. Figure 3 shows a wavefront heading toward a surface. The wavefront is perpendicular to the light ray, like a line of marchers walking side by side.

As each point along the wavefront reaches the surface, it bounces off. All the points travel at the same speed, so they all cover the same total distance in the same time. That means the wavefront as a whole leaves the surface at an angle equal to the angle it came in.

Notice that wavelength plays no part in this. A surface reflects red, green, and blue light all in the same direction.

5.title: Specular and Diffuse Reflection
5.text:
Specular and Diffuse Reflection

Specular reflection sends parallel rays off in parallel; diffuse reflection scatters them in many directions.

Look at the left side of Figure 4. Parallel light rays hit a mirror and leave still parallel. That only happens when the surface isn't rough on the scale of the light's wavelength, and we call such a surface smooth. Reflection from a smooth surface, where parallel rays reflect in parallel, is called specular reflection.

Now the right side. A sheet of paper looks smooth to you, but on the scale of a light wave, it's actually quite rough. Parallel rays hit it and bounce off in all sorts of directions. This scattering of light off a rough surface is called diffuse reflection.

The law of reflection still works on rough surfaces. Each ray's angle of reflection still equals its angle of incidence. The difference is that, up close, the normals at different spots on the paper point in different directions, so the reflected rays scatter. And that answers our focus question: a mirror keeps the rays organized, so you see your face, while paper scrambles them, so no matter how much light it reflects, it can never act as a mirror.

6.title: Objects and Plane-Mirror Images
6.text:
Objects and Plane-Mirror Images

A plane mirror is a flat, smooth surface that reflects light by specular reflection.

A plane mirror, like the one you look into each morning, is a flat, smooth surface that reflects light by specular reflection.

When we study light, an object is either a luminous source, which makes its own light, like a lightbulb, or an illuminated source, which reflects light from something else, like a person. Light usually spreads out from an object in all directions.

Look at the woman in Figure 5. She is illuminated: light from the room lights up her face, and her skin reflects that light diffusely, in every direction. Some of it reaches the mirror, and the mirror reflects it specularly, so an image appears.

7.title: Virtual Images
7.text:
Virtual Images

A virtual image is formed by diverging light rays that only seem to come from behind the mirror.

In Figure 6, light reflects diffusely from every part of the bird, which is our object. The girl sees the light that bounces off the mirror into her eye. Her brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it traces the rays backward along the dashed lines. The light seems to come from a point behind the mirror.

Just as the rays spread out from the bird, they also seem to spread out from that point behind the mirror. The combination of these rays forms the bird's image. It's a virtual image, a type of image formed by diverging light rays.

A virtual image is always on the opposite side of the mirror from the object, and no light actually reaches the image location. That's what makes it virtual. Plane mirrors produce only virtual images.

8.title: Example Problem 1, Changing the Angle of Incidence
8.text:
Example Problem 1, Changing the Angle of Incidence

Rotating a mirror by an angle turns the reflected ray through twice that angle.

A light ray strikes a plane mirror at 52.0 degrees to the normal. The mirror then rotates 35.0 degrees around the point where the ray hits, so the angle of incidence decreases. The rotation axis is perpendicular to the plane of the rays. What is the angle between the first reflected ray and the final reflected ray?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the situation before the mirror rotates. Draw a second sketch with the mirror rotated, and a third showing both reflected rays. Known: the initial angle of incidence is 52.0 degrees, and the mirror's rotation is 35.0 degrees. Unknown: the change in the angle of the reflected ray.

Step two: solve. For the angle of incidence to get smaller, the mirror rotates clockwise. The final angle of incidence is the initial angle minus the mirror's rotation: 52.0 degrees minus 35.0 degrees, or 17.0 degrees clockwise from the new normal. By the law of reflection, the final angle of reflection equals the final angle of incidence, so it's 17.0 degrees counterclockwise from the new normal. Using the sketches, the reflected ray's rotation equals the initial angle of reflection plus the mirror's rotation minus the final angle of reflection: 52.0 degrees plus 35.0 degrees minus 17.0 degrees, which is 70.0 degrees clockwise from the original direction.

Step three: evaluate. Comparing the first and last sketches, the angle between the light ray and the normal shrinks as the mirror turns clockwise. So it makes sense that the reflected ray also turns clockwise, and that it turns through 70.0 degrees, twice the mirror's 35.0 degree rotation.

9.title: Image Position and Height
9.text:
Image Position and Height

For a plane mirror, x sub i equals negative x sub o, and h sub i equals h sub o.

Your mirror image looks just as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it, standing the same way up and matching your size. That's where the phrase mirror image comes from. Figure 7 shows why. Two rays from point O, the tip of a candle flame, hit the mirror at points P one and P two. Ray 1 hits at an angle of incidence of zero degrees, so it bounces straight back on itself. Ray 2 hits at an angle and reflects at the same angle from the normal.

Extend the reflected rays behind the mirror as dashed sight lines. They meet at point I, the image of point O. The geometry makes two congruent triangles, O P one P two and I P one P two. So the distance from the object to the mirror, x sub o, equals the distance from the image to the mirror. That's why x sub i equals negative x sub o: the image is the same distance away, and the negative sign tells us it's behind the mirror, so it's virtual.

Draw rays from the bottom of the candle too, and their sight lines meet at the bottom of the image. The same congruent-triangle reasoning shows that image height equals object height: h sub i equals h sub o. The same is true of every other dimension of the object. So a plane-mirror image is virtual, upright, the same size as the object, and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

10.title: Image Orientation
10.text:
Image Orientation

A plane mirror keeps up and down the same but gives a front-to-back reversal.

A plane mirror gives an image with the same orientation as the object. Stand upright, and your image stands upright. Do a headstand, and your image does one too.

But there is one change: a front-to-back reversal. Follow the sight lines in Figure 8. The image is behind the mirror, facing the boy. When he raises his right hand, it looks like the image raises its left. Yet from the boy's own point of view, the raised hand is still on his right side. The mirror doesn't actually swap left and right. It only flips the image so it faces the opposite direction.

11.title: Career Connection, Set Designer
11.text:
Career Connection, Set Designer

Set designers use reflection, refraction, color, and brightness to create mood on stage.

Ever noticed eerie lighting effects at a school play or a concert? Someone designed those. Set designers for theaters, movies, and concerts use what they know about light, including reflection, refraction, color, intensity, and brightness, to create mood and special effects. Your understanding of mirrors could one day light up a stage.
